source.title: Deep Transformers with Latent Depth
source.authors: Xian Li; Asa Cooper Stickland; Yu-Qing Tang; X. Kong

record.tranche_reason: Reports results on training deep Transformers, an NLP setting outside the claim versions’ specified tasks and architectures.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Transformer training stability and translation or language-modeling metrics, not training classification error on CIFAR benchmarks. Its findings are adjacent but do not test any listed version’s stated measure or setting.
record.test_reason: The study measures training stability and predictive quality in residual Transformers using learned layer selection. None of V1–V6 names this intervention and system combination. In particular, it does not compare plain convolutional networks with identity-shortcut networks, manipulate initialization, or test batch normalization or learning-rate stability thresholds.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that learned latent depth enables stable training of deeper Transformers and improves quality in their translation and masked-language-modeling experiments. Quality improvements are not uniform: the 96-layer latent model has worse held-out perplexity than the static 48-layer model.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains Transformers for machine translation and masked language modeling using learned latent layer selection; it does not evaluate the claim’s gradient-training recipes or classification-error outcomes.
record.method_sensitivity: Static-depth 96-layer masked-language model training diverged both with and without LayerDrop, while latent layers trained successfully; static 24-layer decoder baselines diverged in the reported multilingual translation setting, while latent-layer models trained successfully.

fits_no_version.finding: Static 96-layer masked-language Transformers diverged with and without LayerDrop, whereas the latent-layer model trained and reached held-out perplexity 2.66.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned latent layer selection can stabilize deep Transformer training in the tested masked-language-modeling setting.

fits_no_version.finding: On O2M-Diverse translation, a static 24-layer decoder diverged, while latent-layer decoders trained successfully at 24 and 100 layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned latent layer selection can enable deeper Transformer decoders to train in the tested multilingual translation setting.

record.problems: The reported outcomes concern NLP loss, perplexity, and translation quality rather than classification error; no results test the listed CIFAR or vision-network versions.

untested.parts: Training classification error of convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random labels and the stated capacity and training-recipe conditions.
Spurious local minima and additional student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth-related training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, prevention by identity shortcuts, and the stated initialization exceptions.
Effects of activation-matched initialization and orthogonal versus Gaussian weights on learning speed and trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to initial stability thresholds, transient loss growth, curvature reduction, edge-of-stability dynamics, and divergence below the threshold.
Batch normalization's effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparable training without normalization using Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: T3 requires a result on a listed claim version; a related depth experiment alone is insufficient. The row states indicate inability to determine those versions, not uncertainty about the reported divergence or successful training. No omitted result in the supplied text directly tests V1–V6.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error; random or corrupted labels; model size, optimizer, and training-duration conditions.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious local minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity residual shortcuts, and the stated CIFAR-10/ImageNet training-error comparison. The paper studies Transformers instead.
The specified activation-matched, orthogonal, and Gaussian initializations and their effects on plain-network learning speed or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and squared-loss training.
Batch-normalization comparisons on the named vision tasks and Fixup residual-network comparisons.

rows.subject: Static depth 96
rows.operation_detail: Trained a 96-layer static-depth encoder for crosslingual masked language modeling.
rows.note: This is a training-stability result, not a classification-error measure.
rows.check: The reported divergence is correctly extracted, but Transformer training divergence does not establish any listed version's effect.

rows.subject: Static 96-layer model with LayerDrop
rows.operation_detail: Trained the static 96-layer encoder using LayerDrop.
rows.note: The paper states that increasing warmup and decreasing learning rate for the static 96-layer model did not fix training-loss divergence.
rows.check: Divergence with 50% LayerDrop is correctly extracted. Appendix C.2 attributes the additional learning-rate and warmup attempts to the static 96-layer model generally, without specifying that they were repeated with LayerDrop.

rows.subject: LL, 96
rows.operation_detail: Trained a 96-layer encoder with latent layers for crosslingual masked language modeling.
rows.baseline: Static 96 and static 96 with LayerDrop: Diverged
rows.note: The result demonstrates stable training in this Transformer setting; perplexity does not measure classification error.
rows.check: Held-out perplexity 2.66 is correct, but it measures predictive quality of the proposed method and cannot establish a listed version's training effect.

rows.subject: Static depth baseline model
rows.operation_detail: Trained a static-depth Transformer with a 24-layer decoder on multilingual translation.
rows.note: The prose says the static-depth baseline diverged; this is not a classification-error result.
rows.check: Static 24-layer decoder divergence is correctly extracted; these Transformers already have residual shortcuts, so this is not the plain-versus-residual comparison in V3.

rows.subject: LL-D, 24-layer decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained a 24-layer decoder using latent layers on multilingual translation.
rows.note: The reported comparison concerns training stability for Transformers.
rows.check: Successful training is correctly extracted, but learned latent layer selection does not test any listed intervention.

rows.subject: LL-D, 100-layer decoder
rows.operation_detail: Trained a 100-layer decoder using latent layers on multilingual translation.
rows.note: The paper reports successful training for the latent-layer model, not classification error.
rows.check: Successful training at 100 decoder layers is correctly extracted, but it does not test the specified architectures or interventions in V3 or V4.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
